kandidaty.zagolovok: Running the full server-side Datasette Python app in the browser with service workers and Pyodide
kandidaty.tekst:
Datasette Lite is my port of the Datasette Python application to run directly in the browser using WebAssembly and Pyodide. I've released a complete rewrite of Datasette Lite using service workers, and it's now almost indistinguishable from the real server-side application.

You can now do all of the following, using a carefully crafted URL to lite.datasette.io:

- Load client-side Datasette to browse any SQLite database, JSON file, CSV file or SQL script

- Select a released version of Datasette to load from PyPI

- Load a specific commit, tag, or branch name from the Datasette GitHub repository

- Pick from over 100 versions of SQLite to use with Datasette

- Install additional Datasette plugins from PyPI or URLs to wheel files, including JavaScript visualization tools

The ability to load specific Datasette references, plugins, and SQLite versions makes this a fantastic tool for linking to demos of work-in-progress features or bug reproductions, without needing to spin up a full web server to serve that demo.

As an example, consider the following URL:

https://lite.datasette.io/?install=datasette-maplibre&url=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/demo.db&metadata=https://gist.githubusercontent.com/simonw/39fa5d399465766039549912e2b3d291/raw/f6dfba99a75cbb8b5d9386223220eb52272767ee/metadata.yml#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent

Follow that link and, after a short loading screen, you'll find yourself on a page that looks like this:

That's Datasette running the new datasette-maplibre plugin, loading up a database of GeoJSON shapes of countries and displaying both a combined map and individual boundary maps in a table.

Let's break down that URL to see what it's doing:

https://lite.datasette.io/
?install=datasette-maplibre
&url=https://.../demo.db
&metadata=https://.../metadata.yml
#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent

The ?install=datasette-maplibre installs that additional plugin from PyPI. You can pass &install=... as many times as you like to load more plugins.

&url=https://.../demo.db loads that SQLite database from the provided URL. These URLs need to have open CORS headers - I host files like this in Gists, because they provide an easy way to get open CORS headers on a web-hosted file.

&metadata=https://.../metadata.yml loads this metadata.yml file. The metadata file adds HTML descriptions to various tables, and to the Datasette homepage. Visit that homepage here for a guided tour of the other features of that plugin, all defined in the metadata file.

#/demo/capitals_and_countries%23map=0/4.2/180&color=continent is a fragment hash that turns into a location within Datasette - here it's loading the /demo/capitals_and_countries SQL view, then appending another fragment hash to it (%23 is a URL-encoded #) which tells the map plugin to zoom to a certain location and to set the color of the shapes on the ma

Release: llm 0.37.3

A bug fix release for LLM, mainly to cover a problem with the most recent Homebrew package of the software.

Homebrew now ships the latest SQLite, 3.54.1, which includes a fix that broke LLM's logging code.

Short version: in SQLite 3.54.0 the following SQL:

select json_object('a', (select json_array(1)))

Returns this:

{"a":[1]}

But in 3.54.1 the same query returns this:

{"a":"[1]"}

According to D. Richard Hipp:

That was a bug fix. Per the documentation, (SELECT json_array(...)) returns SQL text, not JSON. Hence the 3.54.1 behavior is correct and 3.54.0 was a bug.

The workaround looks like this:

select json_object('a', json((select json_array(1))))

Tags: llm, webassembly, sqlite, generative-ai, ai, llms, d-richard-hipp

kandidaty.zagolovok: Productiv-icky
kandidaty.tekst:
productiv-icky (adj.) - the feeling of doing work you didn’t mean to do

We have a problem.

full interactive post is here

We agree this is insane, right? Someone I don’t know sends me emails that I’m expected to reply to. I don’t know them. I don’t work for them.

So I ignore them (well actually I send them to email jail). Nuh-uh, that’s not my work, buddy.

But it’s different if it’s my super-intelligent, helpful agent friend…

Yeses are easy. They’re quick.

But every yes has a yes-tax. The hidden extra work you didn’t think of. The long tail of regret where you question why you ever said yes.

Say I did reply to those emails, they’d send me stuff to read to show how great they are at their job and how much better I’d be. Then we’d organise a call (which would derail whichever day that call was on). Then we’d have follow-up items. Then a string of other crap I couldn’t care less about.

I know what’s going to happen. I can smell it, it stinks. I’ve said yes and paid the tax many times before. Now I pay $200/mo for a super-intelligent, over-eager, needy little nerd to ping me incessantly about taking things off my plate.

I feel bad for him. He wants to work. He’s gagging for it. Just. One. More. Task. Master.

Plus, my little nerd has a gambling problem. Or rather, he feeds mine.

Remember years ago sending tons of Slack messages to get the most out of your $20/mo plan? Nor me. Why? Because it’s dumb. But now we feel like we should use all our tokens before they run out. Why? Because everyone else is.

We started measuring shovels instead of the hole.

Someone’s needy little nerd booked their dentist, replied to their mum and launched a business whilst they were asleep. They’ve got an org chart. For nerds. With a Chief of Staff.

You feel behind. Like way behind.

So you grab a shovel and start digging. A little hole over there to triage your inbox, one here to draft your tweets, one to check on those. Then you spend your day checking the holes are being dug right. Before long, you’re surrounded by holes and a mountain of dirt you gotta do something with.

Now as a man, holes are hardwired into my DNA. A few beers, a beach and a shovel, I’m digging a hole.

I’d take pride in it. I’d make the best one, impressively round, deep enough to see sea water seep through the bottom.

But I’d only dig one. There’s a whole beach but I chose this spot.

Next time the needy little nerd pings you: do you really want another hole?

Also, don’t dig big holes on the beach. They collapse.

@swyx: devin bots are multi-agent teams done right:
- always on, proactive (but tuned for ROI)
- own outcomes not tasks (but can collab w others)
- manages teams of subagents (and reviews itself)
- available everywhere (call text slack whatever hello @interaction)

this is the preview that @walden_yan gave at AIE. i've been trialing them for a week and i've been able to hand over my AEO, QA, cross-platform app porting, personal admin automation, and video editing work (also simultaneously moving from local agent worktree hell to cloud because ofc this is all cloud based thank god)

hyped concepts this replaces:
- /goal
- "ultracode" / "ultra mode"
- "loop engineering"
- "agent to agent"
- "agent swarms"
- AI employees (see below)

my main aha moment is that you don't want "AI Employees", we do not have agi yet and you will just fail if you overpromise/overexpect. what you want is the "just" the next level of abstraction above single tasks, and the overwhelming consensus I've had talking to everyone at the frontier of agents (yes incl cog competitors) is agent managers that own outcomes. 

incidentally, as an employer of humans it's also how i distinguish between someone who "has agency" (owns a problem area, finds issues and researches/brings solutions not problems) and who doesn't (only does precisely what i asked, not proactive, doesn't come up with suggestions i didn't think about). guess which one i value more lol.

@testingcatalog: August has launched “Instinct for Healthcare”, allowing August agent to call a doctor's office and book an appointment on behalf of a patient. 

August is an AI-powered health and wellness companion designed to help users interpret medical data, analyze symptoms, and navigate healthcare.

The agent can book appointments, handle insurance claims and prescription refills, giving users access to the full transcript of the calls it makes.

Цитирует @anuruddh_m: We raised $12M from @Accel and @PeakXV to put AI through the bullshit American healthcare puts you through.

Navigating healthcare is hard and all of us have a list of healthcare tasks we’ve been putting off. From visiting a doctor to filing an insurance claim, the tasks pile up and get put off.

We’ve already helped 10M people understand their health. August now talks to the health system on your behalf. Tell it what you need, and August takes care of it.

In the last few weeks, August spent 24,286 minutes on hold while finding the earliest available in-network doctor appointments for our early users.

It spent 366 minutes on hold for one person alone. It also helped another save $1,255 on an insurance claim. Naturally, the ones who tried it say that they can't ever imagine going back.

I’ve held the phone for hours calling doctors, while a disease made it hard to even hold the phone. I’ve felt lost and overwhelmed when dealing with a disease and the system. 

It’s why I started building August, so that all of us have a companion for our health.
